title: Drop by drop
hookLine: as a water jar fills drop by drop, so goodness gathers little by little (Dhammapada 122)
tomorrow: what made the Buddha stop a fight between two groups of monks?
last: THE PATH · EARNEST · MY OWN LIST

lines: A LEAKY FAUCET, A FULL GLASS.
A RICH MAN WHO GAVE ALMOST NOTHING.
cards: A leaky faucet at night: one drop, then another, and by morning the glass under it is full. That's the whole answer to how a jar fills from a tap that only drips.

Verse one twenty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about goodness. And its story starts with a rich man who gave almost nothing.

teach.h: DOOR TO DOOR FOR ONE MEAL.
teach.b: The commentary tells it. A man in Savatthi went door to door gathering food so the whole town could offer one meal to the Buddha and his monks.

teach.h: A PINCH OF RICE, MIXED IN ANYWAY.
teach.b: At a rich man's house he was given a pinch of rice, a drop of butter, a little honey: a gift so small it was nearly an insult. He didn't sneer.

He mixed those few grains into the big pots with everyone else's, and wished the rich man well for his share. The rich man had come to watch, expecting to be mocked. He heard the blessing instead, and asked forgiveness.

teach.h: DROP BY DROP THE POT FILLS.
teach.b: The Buddha spoke the verse: don't think lightly of good, saying it won't come to me; drop by drop the pot fills, and the wise fill up with good little by little.
Buddhists call what gathers that way merit, punna in Pali, and many make it in small daily acts: a spoonful of rice in a monk's bowl, a flower at a shrine, a kind word, often dedicated to others.
The verse's own point: no good is too small to count.

how: Buddhists speak of making merit (punna) through small, regular acts: giving food to monks on their alms round, offering flowers or light at a shrine, keeping precepts, and dedicating the merit to others.

o: a rite of pouring water to honor the dead
goodness that gathers little by little over time
giving one large gift so you're done for the year

games.q: the week's verses: tap the pairs.
p: I have stopped; you stop too
the rich man's pinch of rice
mixed in anyway, drop by drop

s: in the story, the collector mocked the rich man's tiny gift
he mixed it in with everyone's and wished him well; the rich man asked forgiveness.
verse 122 says even small good fills you up over time
even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled.
merit in Buddhism only comes from big, costly gifts
a spoonful of rice, a flower, a kind word: small acts make merit too.

games.q: you're collecting food for the Buddha's meal. a rich man hands you a pinch of rice and a drop of butter. what do you do?
o: hand it back politely; it won't make a difference.
tell the town how little he gave, so he'll feel ashamed.
mix it into the pots with the rest, and wish him well.
games.why: the collector mixed it in and wished him merit. the rich man, who'd come expecting mockery, asked forgiveness.

practice: Count small good things from this week, one for each breath: a door held, a text answered, a cup of tea someone made. Let each one fall like a drop. Don't hunt for big ones; the small ones are the point.

wordCard.voice: Drop by drop: goodness gathered little by little, the way a water-pot fills from a dripping tap.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: punna, merit, the good that gathers from good acts.

carryVoice: Your line: drop by drop, and no drop too small. One week inside the Dhammapada, seven lines in the jar.
